title: Rhoda at the door (Acts 12:1–17)
hookLine: Peter escapes prison, knocks, and the maid is so happy she forgets to open

cards: This one starts dark. King Herod, a later Herod than the one in the Christmas story, has James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword.
Seeing it pleases some people, he arrests Peter too, during Passover week, planning a public trial after the festival. Four squads of soldiers guard him.

The night before the trial he's asleep between two of them, chained to both. Across the city, in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, the church is gathered, praying for him deep into the night.
In the King James Bible: "prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him." Hold on to that. They're praying for this.

teach.b: In the prison, a light. An angel nudges Peter in the side: get up, quickly. The chains fall off his wrists.
Put on your belt, the angel says, and your sandals. Now your cloak. Follow me.
Peter follows, half asleep, sure he's dreaming: past the first guard, past the second, to the iron gate into the city, which opens by itself. They walk one street, and the angel is gone.
Peter comes to himself: this is real. So he goes to Mary's house and knocks at the outer gate. A servant girl named Rhoda, which means rose, comes to answer.

teach.h: SHE OPENED NOT THE GATE FOR GLADNESS.
teach.b: Here's Luke's line: "And when she knew Peter's voice, she opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in, and told how Peter stood before the gate." She's so happy she forgets to open the door.
And the room full of people praying for Peter's release says, in the King James: "Thou art mad." She insists. Then it must be his angel, they say.
Meanwhile, outside, a wanted man stands in the street: "But Peter continued knocking."

When they open it, they're astonished. Two things to notice. Luke gives the servant girl a name: in a story full of kings, soldiers and apostles, the one who recognizes the voice is Rhoda, and she's remembered.
And the church prayed hard, but when the answer came, it was standing on the doorstep, and they almost didn't let it in.

how: Christians often tell the story of Rhoda with a smile, as a picture of praying hard and then being surprised by the answer. Catholics and others read Peter's escape on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, June 29.

games.q: you're Rhoda. it's the middle of the night, someone's knocking, and you know that voice: it's Peter, who's supposed to be in prison. what do you do?
o: run inside to tell everyone, leaving the gate shut.
ask him to prove who he is.
games.why: she opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in. the room told her she was mad, and Peter continued knocking.

practice: Look back over the last month for something good you'd hoped for that arrived, and that you nearly missed or didn't believe at first: a message left unread, good news you second-guessed, a kindness you assumed must be a mistake.
Let yourself smile at it, or laugh, the way you'd laugh at Rhoda running in with the door still shut. If you pray, you can say thank you.

wordCard.voice: Rose. What the name Rhoda means, the servant girl so glad to hear Peter's voice at the door that she forgot to let him in.

orig.note: Greek: rose. The name of the servant girl who knew Peter's voice.
